I understand what he's saying, but he falls short of being completely right in so many ways:

For starters, if virtue is measured on a harm/benefit scale (which is what he's implying when he says that a monster not doing harm is virtuous, while a rabbit is not virtuous due to lack of impact), then someone who isn't exceptionally harmful, but is capable of acts which benefit people greatly, would be considered virtuous. You could argue a step further that someone who is capable of great benefit is therefore morally obligated to do so, so their failure to do so is in effect a great harm, bringing us back to square one - but I'd say at that point we're just arguing semantics.

Next, when people talk about virtues, they will often be talking about things like trustworthiness, kindness, etc. In many cases, these virtues will do more to mitigate nuisance then to mitigate actual harm. And while the consistent practice of certain virtues may lead to situations where they help avoid a harm, they're typically still considered virtues even when they don't.

Which leads to the next point, even if we're specifically talking about virtue in the context of harm, the harm doesn't have to originate from the virtuous person. Harm can be embedded within nature itself, or come from other people. If the virtuous person can help people avoid the harm, they're still virtuous.

But let's go back to the idea of what kind of harm a person is capable of. We've mentioned that trustworthiness is often considered a virtue. Now, let's suppose that we're talking about a person who isn't trustworthy because they regularly tell white lies. And let's suppose that they're graceful enough that no single lie of theirs is actually harmful to anyone. Yet if the same person was completely trustworthy, their trustworthiness would be considered a virtue. Why, if in the first case, they weren't actually causing harm? I'd say the difference is that if you can reliably trust someone always, it's a useful thing because you know you're on solid ground with their words, so there's a material difference between the two versions of the same person.

I'll conclude by saying be kind to the bunnies, at least until it's time to eat them: the bunny that you're talking about may share it's food with its brothers and sisters, which may not mean much to you, but which would make a difference to them. Because even if the virtue of a particular bunny may not show on the scale at which you're viewing the world, it doesn't mean that it's not there at a certain level. And if it's there at the bunny level, then the exact same mentality would also work at the human level, ergo it still makes sense to call the bunny virtuous.

TL;DR: if you buy into his oversimplified assumptions it kind of makes sense.
